parsed_answer.content: Exactly-once delivery in Apache Kafka is a common point of confusion that often stems from a misunderstanding of the distributed systems CAP theorem constraints. Technically, Kafka does not provide a 'magic' exactly-once delivery guarantee for the entire end-to-end pipeline; instead, it provides exactly-once semantics (EOS) for the producer-to-broker and read-process-write cycles. This is achieved through a combination of idempotent producers and atomic transactions. An idempotent producer ensures that retries caused by network blips do not result in duplicate records on the broker by assigning a producer ID and a monotonically increasing sequence number to each batch. When combined with the transaction API, Kafka allows a producer to send a set of messages to multiple partitions such that they are either all committed or none are, effectively solving the 'zombie' producer problem and ensuring atomic state transitions.

items: Idempotent Producers: The broker maintains a sequence number per Producer ID (PID) and partition. If a sequence number is less than or equal to the last committed number, the broker rejects the write as a duplicate.

Transactional API: Uses a Transaction Coordinator and a __transaction_state internal topic to track the status of a transaction. It leverages a two-phase commit protocol to ensure that offsets and output records are committed atomically.

Zombie Fencing: Kafka uses an epoch (producer epoch) to fence off older instances of a producer. If a producer attempts to commit a transaction with an expired epoch, the broker throws a ProducerFencedException, preventing split-brain scenarios.
Consumer Isolation: Consumers must set isolation.level to 'read_committed' to ensure they only see messages from successfully completed transactions, ignoring aborted ones.

parsed_answer.content: The biggest 'gotcha' is that Kafka's EOS only covers the Kafka-to-Kafka pipeline. If your consumer writes to an external database, you are back to at-least-once territory unless you implement a distributed transaction or use an idempotent database schema (e.g., upserts based on a unique business key). Never assume that enabling EOS in Kafka magically makes your entire microservice architecture atomic.
